claims.evidence: This is cited from Lombraña et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The proportion of cells in S phase is substantially lower in stationary phase cells compared with exponentially growing L. major cells.
claims.source: Flow cytometry showed that the proportion of cells in S phase (with DNA content between 1C and 2C) was substantially lower in a population of stationary cells compared with exponentially growing cells (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Stationary phase L. major cells incorporate very low levels of IdU or EdU.
claims.source: Concomitantly, stationary phase cells, unlike exponentially growing cells, incorporated very low levels of IdU or EdU (Figure 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by IdU and EdU incorporation assays in Figure 1B and C.

claims.claim: L. major cells in stationary phase perform little detectable DNA synthesis.
claims.source: Thus, L. major cells in stationary phase perform little detectable DNA synthesis and were therefore deemed suitable to be used as a non-replicative sample in MFA-seq analysis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the flow cytometry and nucleotide incorporation data in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Subtelomeric enrichment in EXP/STA MFA-seq could not be explained by loss of read coverage in these regions in STA cells.
claims.source: Subtelomeric enrichment in EXP/STA could not be explained by loss of read coverage in these regions of the chromosomes in STA cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and though the MFA-seq signal was more clearly detected when the data were analysed by Z score (Figure 1—figure supplements 3, 4 and 5), the same pattern was discernible when analysing copy-number variation (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The subtelomeric MFA-seq signal was most clearly seen in the larger chromosomes in ES/STA mapping.
claims.source: In ES/STA MFA-seq mapping, the amplitude of subtelomeric MFA-seq signal was lower than the more central MFA-seq peak in each chromosome and, indeed, was most clearly seen in the larger chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is observed from the MFA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The subtelomeric MFA-seq signal was notably stronger in G1/STA and G2/STA MFA-seq mapping.
claims.source: However, the subtelomeric MFA-seq signal was notably stronger in G1/STA and G2/STA MFA-seq mapping of all chromosomes, where the central MFA-seq peak was much less pronounced.
claims.evidence: This is observed from the MFA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Sites of subtelomeric DNA synthesis appear spatially separate from previously mapped, predominantly chromosome-central regions of DNA replication initiation.
claims.source: First, sites of subtelomeric DNA synthesis, predicted by change in sequence copy number, appear spatially separate from previously mapped, predominantly chromosome-central regions of DNA replication initiation (Marques et al., 2015) and can be found in virtually every L. major chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the MFA-seq data showing distinct peaks at chromosome ends versus centers.

claims.claim: Predicted subtelomeric DNA replication initiation can be found in virtually every L. major chromosome.
claims.source: First, sites of subtelomeric DNA synthesis, predicted by change in sequence copy number, appear spatially separate from previously mapped, predominantly chromosome-central regions of DNA replication initiation (Marques et al., 2015) and can be found in virtually every L. major chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is observed from the MFA-seq data across all chromosomes.

claims.claim: A single replication initiation region in each L. major chromosome is activated early in S phase.
claims.source: Second, whereas a single replication initiation region in each L. major chromosome is activated early in S phase, predicted subtelomeric DNA replication initiation can be detected in all enriched stages of the L. major cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is shown by the ES/STA MFA-seq data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Predicted subtelomeric DNA replication initiation can be detected in all enriched stages of the L. major cell cycle.
claims.source: Second, whereas a single replication initiation region in each L. major chromosome is activated early in S phase, predicted subtelomeric DNA replication initiation can be detected in all enriched stages of the L. major cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is shown by the MFA-seq data across G1, ES, LS, and G2/M in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: In ES and LS cells, MFA-seq signal appeared to be found mainly in the internal regions of the chromosomes.
claims.source: In ES and LS, MFA-seq signal appeared to be found mainly in the internal regions of the chromosomes (completely overlapping previously mapped ES/G2 MFA-seq peaks), while signal was strongest proximal to the chromosome ends during G1 and G2/M.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the meta-analysis in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: MFA-seq signal was strongest proximal to the chromosome ends during G1 and G2/M.
claims.source: In ES and LS, MFA-seq signal appeared to be found mainly in the internal regions of the chromosomes (completely overlapping previously mapped ES/G2 MFA-seq peaks), while signal was strongest proximal to the chromosome ends during G1 and G2/M.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the meta-analysis in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In EXP and ES cells, MFA-seq peaks fell into three clusters based on their position in chromosomes.
claims.source: In both EXP and ES cells, MFA-seq was seen as peaks of very consistent amplitude and width that fell into three clusters, one where the peak was found centrally in the chromosomes, and two others where the peak was displaced towards the right or left ends of the chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the meta-analysis in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: There was no obvious separation of MFA-seq peak localisation into the three clusters based on chromosome size.
claims.source: There was no obvious separation of peak localisation into the three clusters based on chromosome size (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: In LS cells, the MFA-seq peaks in each cluster had increased in width.
claims.source: In LS cells (Figure 2B), the MFA-seq peaks in each cluster had increased in width, again to a very consistent extent, with half of the peaks from the less central clusters having merged with the chromosome ends.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The MFA-seq data are consistent with bidirectional progression of replication forks emanating from a single predominant region in each chromosome.
claims.source: These data are consistent with bidirectional progression of replication forks emanating from a single predominant region in each chromosome and suggest considerable consistency in rate or pattern of fork movement irrespective of initiation site.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of MFA-seq peak expansion shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The MFA-seq data suggest considerable consistency in rate or pattern of fork movement irrespective of initiation site.
claims.source: These data are consistent with bidirectional progression of replication forks emanating from a single predominant region in each chromosome and suggest considerable consistency in rate or pattern of fork movement irrespective of initiation site.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the consistent pattern of MFA-seq peak expansion.

claims.claim: In G2/M and G1 cells, the three MFA-seq clusters overlapped to a much greater extent.
claims.source: Finally, in G2/M and G1 cells, the three clusters overlapped to a much greater extent, with MFA-seq signal again showing a consistent pattern across the genome, but here the signal peaked at the chromosome ends and reduced in amplitude towards the interior of the molecules (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In G2/M and G1 cells, MFA-seq signal peaked at the chromosome ends and reduced in amplitude towards the interior.
claims.source: Finally, in G2/M and G1 cells, the three clusters overlapped to a much greater extent, with MFA-seq signal again showing a consistent pattern across the genome, but here the signal peaked at the chromosome ends and reduced in amplitude towards the interior of the molecules (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The time to complete chromosome replication in L. major is size-dependent.
claims.source: Given the range of chromosome sizes in the L. major genome (~0.25–2.4 Mb), a prediction of the mapping is that the time to complete chromosome replication will be size-dependent. To test this prediction, we estimated the extent of each chromosome that is replicated in early S phase by comparing the ES/STA MFA-seq ratios with G2/STA ratios, revealing a greater extent of DNA replication in smaller chromosomes relative to the larger (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the replication timing analysis in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: Smaller L. major chromosomes show a greater extent of DNA replication in early S phase relative to larger chromosomes.
claims.source: To test this prediction, we estimated the extent of each chromosome that is replicated in early S phase by comparing the ES/STA MFA-seq ratios with G2/STA ratios, revealing a greater extent of DNA replication in smaller chromosomes relative to the larger (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Significant differences in replication timing were seen when chromosomes were separated into three size groupings.
claims.source: To explore this further, we separated the chromosomes into three size groupings and significant differences in replication timing were clearly seen (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Simultaneous co-localisation of AcH3, base J and KKT1 was found at the single MFA-seq peak seen in ES cells in every chromosome.
claims.source: As exemplified by chromosome 35 (Figure 3A), simultaneous co-localisation of AcH3, base J and KKT1 was found at the single MFA-seq peak seen in ES cells in every chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and meta-analysis in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Co-localisation of AcH3, base J and KKT1 included MFA-seq peaks at six sites where the surrounding multigene transcription units converge.
claims.source: Surprisingly, this co-localisation included MFA-seq peaks at six sites where the surrounding multigene transcription units converge, and at the telomere of chromosome 1; in each case these are locations of transcription termination, where AcH3 enrichment is not predicted (Thomas et al., 2009), but modest AcH3 enrichment was seen in all cases (Figure 3B, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Modest AcH3 enrichment was seen at transcription termination sites where it is not predicted.
claims.source: Surprisingly, this co-localisation included MFA-seq peaks at six sites where the surrounding multigene transcription units converge, and at the telomere of chromosome 1; in each case these are locations of transcription termination, where AcH3 enrichment is not predicted (Thomas et al., 2009), but modest AcH3 enrichment was seen in all cases (Figure 3B, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 5, with reference to Thomas et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The simultaneous presence of AcH3, base J and KKT1 is a local driver for coordinated DNA replication initiation at a single region in each chromosome in ES.
claims.source: These data suggest that the simultaneous presence of these three genome factors is a local driver for coordinated DNA replication initiation at a single region in each chromosome in ES but does not promote DNA replication initiation in other cell cycle stages.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the meta-analysis in Figure 3C showing strong correlation in ES but not other stages.

claims.claim: The simultaneous presence of AcH3, base J and KKT1 does not promote DNA replication initiation in cell cycle stages other than ES.
claims.source: These data suggest that the simultaneous presence of these three genome factors is a local driver for coordinated DNA replication initiation at a single region in each chromosome in ES but does not promote DNA replication initiation in other cell cycle stages.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the meta-analysis in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Base J itself has little correlation with DNA replication in any cell cycle stage.
claims.source: Meta-analysis of MFA-seq at all sites where base J was found, alone or in combination with AcH3, showed that the modified base itself has little correlation with DNA replication in any cell cycle stage (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the meta-analysis in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: MFA-seq peaks around non-telomeric AcH3 regions were notably smaller in amplitude and narrower in width compared with telomere-proximal AcH3 sites.
claims.source: However, MFA-seq peaks around non-telomeric AcH3 regions were notably smaller in amplitude and narrower in width compared with the pronounced MFA-seq signal around telomere-proximal AcH3 sites.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the meta-analysis in Figure 3C comparing internal and end AcH3 sites.

claims.claim: Fewer AcH3 sites are used for DNA replication initiation in the chromosome interiors compared to subtelomeres.
claims.source: These data provide confirmation of a genome-wide association between AcH3 sites and DNA replication initiation throughout the cell cycle, but it appears that while AcH3 sites are associated with DNA replication initiation in the chromosome subtelomeres, fewer AcH3 sites are used in the chromosome interiors.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the difference in MFA-seq signal amplitude between internal and end AcH3 sites.

claims.claim: Increased copy-number variation in the proximity of chromosome ends was seen in G1 relative to ES, LS and G2.
claims.source: In both cases, increased copy-number variation in the proximity of chromosome ends was seen in G1 relative to ES, LS and G2.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Subtelomeric regions serve as DNA replication initiation sites with relatively higher usage during G1.
claims.source: This further demonstrates that these regions serve as DNA replication initiation sites, and that such sites seem to have a relatively higher usage during G1.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Subtelomere DNA replication initiation is mainly not activated during ES but is a persistent activity throughout the enriched cell cycle populations.
claims.source: Therefore, these data indicate that subtelomere DNA replication initiation is mainly not activated during ES but is a persistent activity throughout the enriched cell cycle populations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the MFA-seq analysis across cell cycle stages.

claims.claim: Local chromatin environment is important in modulating L. major DNA replication initiation in a temporal manner.
claims.source: Altogether, these observations indicate the importance of local chromatin environment in modulating L. major DNA replication initiation in a temporal manner.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential behavior of AcH3 sites in different genomic contexts and cell cycle stages.

claims.claim: MEME analysis retrieved motifs associated with transcription initiation and termination at sites of DNA replication initiation.
claims.source: As expected, MEME analysis retrieved motifs that have been associated with transcription initiation and termination, known to take place at these sites (G/T rich motifs and polypyrimidine tracks; Figure 3—figure supplement 4; Clayton, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and cited from Clayton, 2019.

claims.claim: No sequence signature was found that correlated specifically with regions of DNA replication initiation in L. major.
claims.source: We could not find any sequence signature that correlated specifically with regions of DNA replication initiation, or that differed between the regions used during ES phase or throughout the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a negative result from the MEME analysis.

claims.claim: The major correlation of base skew in L. major is with transcription direction, in which the coding strand is mainly associated with positive G skew and negative T skew values.
claims.source: Our analysis did not indicate such a broad replication-associated pattern, but instead revealed that the major correlation of base skew in L. major is with transcription direction, in which the coding strand is mainly associated with positive G skew and negative T skew values (Figure 4A), as previously reported (El-Sayed et al., 2005; McDonagh et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and cited from El-Sayed et al., 2005 and McDonagh et al., 2000.

claims.claim: A highly localised pattern of polarity change in G and T skew values was found across the centre of the regions of AcH3/base J/KKT1 enrichment.
claims.source: However, a closer examination of the skew patterns in the central area of the ES MFA-seq peaks revealed a highly localised pattern of polarity change, resembling the wider pattern seen around origins of replication in other organisms (see zoomed region in chromosomes 30 and 31; Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The local change in G and T skew values across AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites could be seen even when two adjacent transcription units are transcribed in the same direction.
claims.source: This local change, from negative to positive in the G and T skew values across the centre of the regions of AcH3/base J/KKT1 enrichment, could be seen even when two adjacent transcription units are transcribed in the same direction (see zoomed region in chromosome 31, which is entirely transcribed unidirectionally; Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B for chromosome 31.

claims.claim: Meta-analysis revealed the same localised pattern of polarity change for both G and T skew when every ES MFA-seq site was compared.
claims.source: Accordingly, meta-analysis revealed the same localised pattern of polarity change, for both G and T skew, when every ES MFA-seq site was compared (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the meta-analysis in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: A similar pattern of base skew polarity change was seen across AcH3 sites near chromosome ends, although less pronounced than at AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites.
claims.source: A similar pattern was seen across AcH3 sites near chromosome ends, although both the amplitude and sharpness of the polarity change in base skew was less pronounced than that seen around AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the meta-analysis in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Only T skew showed polarity change around chromosome-internal AcH3 sites.
claims.source: In contrast, only T skew showed the same global polarity change around chromosome-internal AcH3 sites (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: No obviously related profile of base skew polarity change was found around either AcH3/base J or base J sites.
claims.source: Finally, we did not find any obviously related profile of base skew polarity change around either AcH3/base J or base J sites (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: There is clear evidence for base composition bias consistent with DNA replication initiation at a central region in each of the 36 L. major chromosomes.
claims.source: These data provide clear evidence for base composition bias, consistent with DNA replication initiation, at a central region in each of the 36 L. major chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the G/T skew analysis at AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites.

claims.claim: Differences in base composition around core and subtelomeric AcH3 sites are indicative of extensive DNA replication initiation at the latter but not the former.
claims.source: In addition, differences in base composition around core and subtelomeric AcH3 sites are indicative of extensive DNA replication initiation at the latter but not the former.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differences in skew patterns shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: G4s have been predicted to colocalise with SNS-seq signal in Leishmania.
claims.source: G4s have been predicted to colocalise with SNS-seq signal in Leishmania (Lombraña et al., 2016), but their relationship with DNA replication initiation regions mapped by MFA-seq has not been explored.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Lombraña et al., 2016.

claims.claim: There is a strong positional preference for G4 distribution around the midpoint where G and T skews change polarity across the AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites.
claims.source: Our analyses showed a strong positional preference for G4 distribution around the midpoint where G and T skews change polarity across the AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites (see zoomed regions in chromosomes 30 and 31, Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and meta-analysis in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Upstream of the midpoint of AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites, a grouping of G4 peaks could be seen on the reverse DNA strand.
claims.source: Upstream of the midpoint of these sites, a grouping of G4 peaks could be seen on the reverse DNA strand, while downstream of the midpoint a similar grouping was seen on the forward strand.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and meta-analysis in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Downstream of the midpoint of AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites, a grouping of G4 peaks could be seen on the forward DNA strand.
claims.source: Upstream of the midpoint of these sites, a grouping of G4 peaks could be seen on the reverse DNA strand, while downstream of the midpoint a similar grouping was seen on the forward strand.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and meta-analysis in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The localised patterns of G4 distribution were reflected in every ES MFA-seq mapped peak with a striking correlation relative to the base skew polarity change.
claims.source: Meta-analysis showed that these localised patterns of G4 distribution were reflected in every ES MFA-seq mapped peak, with a striking correlation relative to the base skew polarity change (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the meta-analysis in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: A similar global pattern of G4 distribution, although more diffuse, was observed around subtelomeric AcH3 sites.
claims.source: A similar global pattern of G4 distribution, although more diffuse, was observed around subtelomeric AcH3 sites (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: At AcH3/base J and base J sites, G4s were arranged as sharp peaks on both the forward and reverse DNA strands that aligned at the central point of enrichment.
claims.source: At all these predicted sites of DNA replication the G4 distribution differed from the pattern seen at chromosome-internal AcH3 sites, as well as at AcH3/base J and base J sites, where G4s were arranged as sharp peaks on both the forward and reverse DNA strands that aligned at the central point of enrichment (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The region of L. major DNA replication initiation predicted by MFA-seq have imprinted, or have been shaped by, distinct local profiles of DNA intra-strand asymmetries and arrangement of G4s.
claims.source: Altogether, these observations indicate that the region of L. major DNA replication initiation predicted by MFA-seq have imprinted, or have been shaped by, distinct local profiles of DNA intra-strand asymmetries and arrangement of G4s.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between MFA-seq peaks and G/T skew and G4 patterns.

claims.claim: The patterns of DNA intra-strand asymmetries and G4s reflect the predicted differences, in space and time, of DNA replication activity at chromosome-internal and subtelomeric regions.
claims.source: Moreover, the patterns of these genome features reflect the predicted differences, in space and time, of DNA replication activity at chromosome-internal and subtelomeric regions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the different patterns observed at internal versus subtelomeric sites.

claims.claim: A pronounced MFA-seq peak was seen at all AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites when comparing ES or EXP cells with STA cells, with no evidence for differential DNA replication initiation activity between different transcription configurations.
claims.source: As expected, at all sites a pronounced MFA-seq peak was seen when comparing ES or EXP cells with STA cells, with no evidence for differential DNA replication initiation activity between them (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The patterns of G skew, T skew and G4 distribution at AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites were mainly dictated by the leading strand of the predicted bidirectional DNA replication fork, not by the lagging strand.
claims.source: However, by separating these sites, it became clear that the patterns of G skew, T skew (Figure 5C) and G4 distribution (Figure 5D) were mainly dictated by the leading strand of the predicted bidirectional DNA replication fork, not by the lagging strand, irrespective of the surrounding transcription direction.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: Leading strand DNA replication and transcription are always co-directional on the same template DNA strand around chromosome-central putative origins.
claims.source: Moreover, the analysis suggested that leading strand DNA replication and transcription are always co-directional on the same template DNA strand around these chromosome-central putative origins.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the analysis in Figure 5.

claims.claim: There is selective pressure to avoid clashes between DNA replisome and RNA polymerase activities at regions of Leishmania DNA replication initiation.
claims.source: Therefore, this analysis advances the correlation between DNA replication initiation activity and local DNA strand asymmetry and G4 distribution and suggests the existence of selective pressure to avoid clashes between DNA replisome and RNA polymerase activities at regions of Leishmania DNA replication initiation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the co-directionality of leading strand replication and transcription.

claims.claim: At only three sites could an extremely mild increase in MFA-seq signal be detected in ES or G2/M cells after HU treatment compared with non-HU treated cells.
claims.source: At only three sites could we detect an extremely mild increase in MFA-seq signal in ES or G2/M cells after HU treatment compared with non-HU treated cells (red arrows in Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: L. major has a very limited capacity to initiate DNA replication from other loci in ES phase beyond the single predominant site.
claims.source: Though all these sites were located at the boundaries of multigene transcription units, like the single predominant ES MFA-seq peak in each chromosome, these data suggest that L. major has a very limited capacity to initiate DNA replication initiation from other loci in ES phase, though when it occurs such a reaction also predominantly localises to sites of transcription initiation or termination.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the HU treatment experiment showing only three new sites.

claims.claim: When additional DNA replication initiation occurs in L. major ES phase, it predominantly localises to sites of transcription initiation or termination.
claims.source: Though all these sites were located at the boundaries of multigene transcription units, like the single predominant ES MFA-seq peak in each chromosome, these data suggest that L. major has a very limited capacity to initiate DNA replication initiation from other loci in ES phase, though when it occurs such a reaction also predominantly localises to sites of transcription initiation or termination.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the location of the three new sites after HU treatment.

claims.claim: Mapping to each chromosome and meta-analysis did not reveal any change in MFA-seq peak profile at AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites in HU treated ES cells.
claims.source: Mapping to each chromosome (Figure 6B), as well as meta-analysis of MFA-seq signal in all chromosomes (Figure 6C), did not reveal any change in MFA-seq peak profile in the HU treated cells, suggesting that DNA replication emanating from these regions is largely unaffected by this level of HU.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and C.

claims.claim: DNA replication emanating from AcH3/base J/KKT1 regions is largely unaffected by HU treatment.
claims.source: Mapping to each chromosome (Figure 6B), as well as meta-analysis of MFA-seq signal in all chromosomes (Figure 6C), did not reveal any change in MFA-seq peak profile in the HU treated cells, suggesting that DNA replication emanating from these regions is largely unaffected by this level of HU.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in MFA-seq signal after HU treatment.

claims.claim: A pronounced decrease in MFA-seq signal at the chromosome ends during G2/M after release from HU was detected in individual chromosomes.
claims.source: In contrast, we saw pronounced changes in subtelomere replication, since a decrease in MFA-seq signal at the chromosome ends during G2/M after release from HU was detected in individual chromosomes (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: A marked loss of MFA-seq signal around the subtelomeric AcH3 sites upon HU treatment was visible as early as in ES.
claims.source: First, a marked loss of MFA-seq signal, visible as early as in ES, was seen around the subtelomeric AcH3 sites upon HU treatment (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2), whereas no such clear effect was seen around chromosome-internal AcH3 sites (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: No clear effect of HU treatment was seen around chromosome-internal AcH3 sites.
claims.source: First, a marked loss of MFA-seq signal, visible as early as in ES, was seen around the subtelomeric AcH3 sites upon HU treatment (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2), whereas no such clear effect was seen around chromosome-internal AcH3 sites (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The HU-induced loss of the replication signal extended for ~50 kb at chromosome ends.
claims.source: Second, meta-analysis of MFA-seq signal at the ends of every chromosome (Figure 6D) showed that the HU-induced loss of the replication signal extended for ~50 kb.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Not all DNA replication initiation sites are equally affected by replication stress, with replication activity proximal to chromosome ends being more susceptible to HU treatment than replication from chromosome-internal regions.
claims.source: These observations reveal that not all DNA replication initiation sites are equally affected by replication stress, with replication activity proximal to chromosome ends being more susceptible to HU treatment than replication from chromosome-internal regions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of HU on subtelomeric versus internal replication.

claims.claim: The data reinforce the suggestion of differences in the nature of DNA replication around subtelomeric AcH3 sites and chromosome-internal AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites.
claims.source: Moreover, the data reinforce the suggestion of differences in the nature of DNA replication around subtelomeric AcH3 sites and chromosome-internal AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivity to HU.

claims.claim: RAD9 and HUS1 are two components of the 9-1-1 clamp, which is a cell cycle checkpoint complex required for replicative DNA synthesis in L. major.
claims.source: RAD9 and HUS1 are two components of the 9-1-1 clamp, which is a cell cycle checkpoint complex required for replicative DNA synthesis in L. major (Damasceno et al., 2016; Damasceno et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Damasceno et al., 2016 and Damasceno et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Both visual inspection of individual chromosomes and meta-analysis showed a dramatic decrease in MFA-seq signal around subtelomeric AcH3 sites and proximal to the chromosome ends in RAD9+/- cells, in both ES and G2/M.
claims.source: Strikingly, both visual inspection of individual chromosomes (Figure 7A) and meta-analysis (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) showed a dramatic decrease in MFA-seq signal around subtelomeric AcH3 sites and proximal to the chromosome ends in RAD9+/- cells, in both ES and G2/M.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A, B, and C.

claims.claim: No obvious change in MFA-seq signal was seen around chromosome-internal AcH3 sites in G2/M RAD9+/- cells.
claims.source: In contrast, no obvious change in MFA-seq signal was seen around chromosome-internal AcH3 sites in G2/M RAD9+/- cells and, even more strikingly, no change in MFA-seq signal around AcH3/base J/KKT1 was detected in the RAD9+/- cells (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: No change in MFA-seq signal around AcH3/base J/KKT1 was detected in the RAD9+/- cells.
claims.source: In contrast, no obvious change in MFA-seq signal was seen around chromosome-internal AcH3 sites in G2/M RAD9+/- cells and, even more strikingly, no change in MFA-seq signal around AcH3/base J/KKT1 was detected in the RAD9+/- cells (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: In HUS1+/- cells, a milder decrease in MFA-seq signal was observed, which was apparent only for the subtelomeric AcH3 sites during G2/M.
claims.source: In HUS1+/- cells, a milder decrease in MFA-seq signal was observed, which was apparent only for the subtelomeric AcH3 sites during G2/M (Figure 7B and Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and C.

claims.claim: Decreased MFA-seq signal near telomeres was seen when directly comparing sequence abundance in G2-enriched populations from both mutants and wild type cells.
claims.source: Consistently, decreased MFA-seq signal near telomeres was also seen when directly comparing sequence abundance in G2-enriched populations from both mutants and wild type (WT) cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: No alteration in the MFA-seq signal was detected around AcH3/base J or base J sites in either RAD9+/- or HUS1+/- mutants.
claims.source: No alteration in the MFA-seq signal was detected around AcH3/base J or base J sites in either of the mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: DNA replication initiation close to chromosome ends, but not at the distinct chromosome-internal initiation regions, requires the action of the 9-1-1 complex.
claims.source: These data indicate DNA replication initiation close to chromosome ends, but not at the distinct chromosome-internal initiation regions, requires the action of the 9-1-1 complex.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of RAD9 and HUS1 deficiency on subtelomeric versus internal replication.

claims.claim: Genome duplication in L. major predominantly starts from a single region in every chromosome in early S phase, proceeding towards the chromosome ends.
claims.source: Our data show that genome duplication predominantly starts from a single region in every chromosome in early S phase, proceeding towards the chromosome ends, consistent with the observed size dependence of L. major chromosome replication timing.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion from the MFA-seq data across cell cycle stages.

claims.claim: Replication of L. major chromosomes is rarely completed by the end of S phase.
claims.source: However, replication of the chromosomes is rarely completed by the end of S phase, and instead either continues from the same sites as cells transit through G2/M back to G1, or new sites of DNA replication initiation are activated in the chromosome subtelomeres during late S phase or in G2/M and G1 stages of the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the MFA-seq data showing continued replication in G2/M and G1.

claims.claim: The paucity of DNA replication initiation that occurs early in S phase in Leishmania is counterbalanced by DNA replication that can extend beyond conventional S phase.
claims.source: In either model, the paucity of DNA replication initiation that occurs early in S phase is counterbalanced by DNA replication that can extend beyond conventional S phase.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: Mitotic DNA repair synthesis (MiDAS) has been documented as a means to complete replication of hard-to-duplicate genome features such as common fragile sites and telomeres.
claims.source: Mitotic DNA repair synthesis (MiDAS) has been documented as a means to complete replication of hard-to-duplicate genome features such as common fragile sites and telomeres (Özer and Hickson, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Özer and Hickson, 2018.

claims.claim: In the unperturbed cell cycles of both yeast and mammalian cells, onset of mitosis has been documented in the presence of under-replicated genomic regions.
claims.source: Moreover, in the unperturbed cell cycles of both yeast (Ivanova et al., 2020; Torres-Rosell et al., 2007) and mammalian cells (Moreno et al., 2016) onset of mitosis has been documented in the presence of under-replicated genomic regions, leading to DNA synthesis in offspring cells.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Ivanova et al., 2020; Torres-Rosell et al., 2007; and Moreno et al., 2016.

claims.claim: DNA synthesis outside S-phase is particularly prevalent in cells exhibiting aneuploidy.
claims.source: However, DNA synthesis outside S-phase is particularly prevalent in cells exhibiting aneuploidy (Minocherhomji et al., 2015; Özer et al., 2018), suggesting it may be less effective at maintaining genome integrity.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Minocherhomji et al., 2015 and Özer et al., 2018.

claims.claim: L. major exhibits constitutive mosaic aneuploidy, at least in parasite cells derived from, or proliferating in the insect vector.
claims.source: Here, we provide evidence that L. major, a eukaryotic organism with constitutive mosaic aneuploidy (at least in parasite cells derived from, or proliferating in the insect vector) (Prieto Barja et al., 2017; Dumetz et al., 2017), achieves full genome duplication using DNA replication that can continue beyond S phase, including G2/M and G1.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Prieto Barja et al., 2017 and Dumetz et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Mitosis and cell division prior to complete genome duplication might not necessarily be an inherent feature of genome maintenance and transmission in eukaryotes.
claims.source: This finding, in a eukaryotic microbe that is evolutionarily distant from yeast and mammals, suggests that mitosis and cell division prior to complete genome duplication might not necessarily be an inherent feature of genome maintenance and transmission in eukaryotes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in L. major.

claims.claim: A reliance on DNA replication outside S phase may explain the widespread aneuploidy found in Leishmania.
claims.source: In addition, a reliance on DNA replication outside S phase may explain the widespread aneuploidy found in Leishmania.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claims.claim: Chromosome subtelomeric DNA replication is mainly detectable at the temporal extremes of the conventional Leishmania S phase.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, our data suggest that chromosome subtelomeric DNA replication is mainly detectable at the temporal extremes of the conventional Leishmania S phase (either very early in S phase, as seen with the G1 enriched population; or very late in S phase, as seen with the G2/M enriched populations), and such regions have been demonstrated to be particularly prone to copy- number variation (Bussotti et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the MFA-seq data and cited from Bussotti et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Subtelomeric regions in Leishmania have been demonstrated to be particularly prone to copy-number variation.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, our data suggest that chromosome subtelomeric DNA replication is mainly detectable at the temporal extremes of the conventional Leishmania S phase (either very early in S phase, as seen with the G1 enriched population; or very late in S phase, as seen with the G2/M enriched populations), and such regions have been demonstrated to be particularly prone to copy- number variation (Bussotti et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Bussotti et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The subtelomeres of T. brucei share little homology between chromosome homologues, at least in part due to rearrangements among VSG genes.
claims.source: Nonetheless, it is notable that subtelomeric compartments of the T. brucei genome share little homology between chromosome homologues, at least in part due to rearrangements among VSG genes (Müller et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Müller et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The subtelomeres of Plasmodium are locations of immune response gene diversification.
claims.source: The subtelomeres of Plasmodium are also locations of immune response gene diversification, and it may therefore be valuable to dissect the timing of their replication.
claims.evidence: This is general knowledge about Plasmodium biology.

claims.claim: If a cell cycle checkpoint is operational in Leishmania, it must be permissive enough to allow cells to undergo mitosis with considerable ongoing DNA replication.
claims.source: If such a checkpoint is operational at all in Leishmania, it must be permissive enough to allow cells to undergo mitosis with considerable ongoing DNA replication.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of DNA replication in G2/M and G1.

claims.claim: The 9-1-1 complex, or its subunits, may participate in a specific DNA replication checkpoint responsible for detecting and protecting replication forks stalled by subtelomeric repeats.
claims.source: Perhaps, in L. major the 9-1-1 complex, or its subunits, participates in a specific DNA replication checkpoint responsible for detecting and protecting replication forks stalled by the subtelomeric repeats, allowing DNA synthesis to continue while undergoing mitosis.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential requirement for 9-1-1 at subtelomeres.

claims.claim: Binding sites of ORC components have not been mapped in the L. major genome.
claims.source: Unlike in T. brucei (Tiengwe et al., 2012a), binding sites of ORC components have not been mapped in the L. major genome, and so it remains to be determined if and how they overlap with the MFA-seq signals we describe.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claims.claim: No functional analysis of the initiator has been described in Leishmania.
claims.source: Indeed, despite conservation of predicted ORC components (Tiengwe et al., 2012b; Tiengwe et al., 2014; Marques and McCulloch, 2018; Marques et al., 2016), no functional analysis of the initiator has been described in Leishmania (da Silva et al., 2017), meaning we cannot rule out innovations in ORC that could provide S-phase-uncoupled licensing and firing of replication initiation sites, allowing DNA replication outside S phase.
claims.evidence: This is cited from da Silva et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The single MFA-seq peak found in each chromosome coincides with KKT1 localised to the boundaries of the transcription units.
claims.source: Nonetheless, this work shows that the single MFA-seq peak found in each chromosome – the only genomic region clearly activated early in S phase – coincides with KKT1 localised to the boundaries of the transcription units.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: In T. brucei, the earliest acting origin in each chromosome is bound by ORC and coincides with the mapped centromere.
claims.source: Here, there is a parallel with T. brucei, where the earliest acting origin in each chromosome is bound by ORC and coincides with the mapped centromere (Tiengwe et al., 2012a), where at least two KKT factors localise (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Tiengwe et al., 2012a and Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014.

claims.claim: Many of the single S-phase MFA-seq peaks in Leishmania are positionally conserved in T. brucei.
claims.source: Moreover, many of the single S-phase MFA-seq peaks in Leishmania are positionally conserved in T. brucei (Marques et al., 2015), arguing that the putative centromere-focused MFA-seq peaks in Leishmania are ORC-defined origins.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Marques et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The subtelomeric regions of intra- and potential post-S-phase DNA replication can only be correlated with AcH3.
claims.source: In contrast, the subtelomeric regions of intra- and potential post-S-phase DNA replication can only be correlated with AcH3, and we cannot be sure that this form of chromatin is actually a determinant of replication initiation; for instance, DNA replication may emanate from the telomeres.
claims.evidence: This is stated as uncertainty about the mechanism of subtelomeric replication.

claims.claim: Subtelomeric DNA replication may not be ORC-derived, but instead derive from DNA repair required for the stability of subtelomeric regions.
claims.source: One possibility is that subtelomeric DNA replication is not ORC-derived, but instead derives from DNA repair that is required for the stability of subtelomeric regions, by either controlling copy-number variation in these regions (Laffitte et al., 2016b) or by directly driving replication initiation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of subtelomeric replication.

claims.claim: The loss of subtelomeric DNA replication in L. major cells deficient in RAD9 may indicate involvement of DNA repair machinery.
claims.source: The loss of subtelomeric DNA replication in L. major cells deficient in RAD9 may provide an insight into the repair machinery involved, since there are parallels with the effects of these mutants and the need for DNA repair activity to direct DNA replication when origins are deleted (Theis et al., 2010) or in conditions of replication stress (Bacal et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the RAD9 mutant data and cited parallels.

claims.claim: MFA-seq analysis has not found association between DNA replication initiation and any specific DNA sequence in L. major.
claims.source: Similar to other eukaryotes, this and previous MFA-seq analysis (Marques et al., 2015), as well as SNS-seq mapping (Lombraña et al., 2016), have not found association between DNA replication initiation and any specific DNA sequence in L. major.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from this and previous studies.

claims.claim: Features related to transcription activity in L. major play a major role in DNA replication initiation.
claims.source: Instead, these studies have consistently suggested that features related to transcription activity in L. major play a major role in DNA replication initiation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between replication sites and transcription boundaries.

claims.claim: Leishmania DNA replication may be initiated in an opportunistic fashion, coupled with transcription initiation and termination events.
claims.source: These findings reinforce the idea that Leishmania DNA replication may be initiated in an opportunistic fashion, coupled with transcription initiation and termination events: an association also seen in other eukaryotes (Lombraña et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2019), although the mechanisms might differ.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data and cited parallels in other eukaryotes.

claims.claim: The ChIP datasets for AcH3, base J and KKT1 lack cell cycle resolution.
claims.source: It should be noted, however, that the ChIP datasets for AcH3, base J and KKT1 lack cell cycle resolution.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the available data.

claims.claim: The order by which AcH3, base J and KKT1 modifications are deposited during the cell cycle may be a major determinant of DNA replication initiation outcomes.
claims.source: Thus, it is possible that the order by which each of these modifications is deposited during the cell cycle is a major determinant of the DNA replication initiation outcomes around them.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Correlation between transcription and GC and AT skews in trypanosomatids has been reported before.
claims.source: Correlation between transcription and GC and AT skews in trypanosomatids has been reported before (El-Sayed et al., 2005; McDonagh et al., 2000) and is mainly a consequence of constitutive transcription in these organisms.
claims.evidence: This is cited from El-Sayed et al., 2005 and McDonagh et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Only the most efficient replication initiation sites in Leishmania were locally imprinted with the skew patterns related to DNA replication initiation activity.
claims.source: Replication is more restricted in time, and thus only the most efficient replication initiation sites (those around AcH3/base J/KKT1 and, to a lesser extent, AcH3 alone) were locally imprinted with the skew patterns related to DNA replication initiation activity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the skew analysis.

claims.claim: The success of using unsorted exponentially growing cells compared with stationary cells for MFA-seq demonstrates its convenience, representing a saving in time and cost.
claims.source: The success of this approach demonstrates its convenience, which represents a saving in time and cost, which may be particularly useful for comparing conditions or mutants predicted to change DNA replication dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage.

claims.claim: The detection of subtelomeric DNA replication provides at least a partial explanation for DNA combing work that has observed two regions of DNA synthesis in a single molecule.
claims.source: While the new approach for MFA-seq described here does not fully resolve the discrepancies in predictions of DNA replication activity by these different methodologies (discussed in recent reviews) (Marques and McCulloch, 2018; da Silva et al., 2017; Rocha-Granados and Klingbeil, 2016), the detection of subtelomeric DNA replication provides at least a partial explanation for DNA combing work that has observed two regions of DNA synthesis in a single molecule (Lombraña et al., 2016; Stanojcic et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the new findings and cited previous work.

claims.claim: Subtelomeric, potentially post-S-phase replication is a core part of genome transmission in Leishmania.
claims.source: More importantly, this work suggests that subtelomeric, potentially post-S-phase replication is a core part of genome transmission in Leishmania, and understanding the nature of this form of DNA replication may have implications for understanding genome plasticity in this microbe, and others.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

results.result: Stationary phase L. major cells show substantially reduced S phase population and minimal DNA synthesis compared to exponentially growing cells, making them suitable as a non-replicative control for MFA-seq analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are well-supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 1A) showing reduced S phase cells and IdU/EdU incorporation assays (Figure 1B,C) demonstrating minimal DNA synthesis in stationary phase cells. The experimental evidence directly supports the conclusion that stationary cells are appropriate controls.

results.result: Previously undetected subtelomeric DNA replication occurs throughout the L. major cell cycle (G1, ES, LS, G2/M), spatially distinct from chromosome-internal replication initiation sites, with signal strongest in G1 and G2/M phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C45-C51 are strongly supported by MFA-seq data in Figures 1D and 2 showing distinct subtelomeric peaks across all cell cycle stages. The spatial separation from internal sites and differential timing are clearly demonstrated. This represents a major novel finding that resolves previous discrepancies in the field.

results.result: MFA-seq reveals a coordinated DNA replication program with three clusters of initiation sites that expand bidirectionally with consistent fork progression rates, independent of chromosome size or initiation site position.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 are supported by meta-analysis in Figure 2A-B showing three distinct clusters with consistent peak expansion patterns. The bidirectional progression and consistent fork movement are well-demonstrated, though the inference about fork rates is indirect from peak width changes.

results.result: Chromosome replication timing in L. major is size-dependent, with smaller chromosomes showing greater extent of replication in early S phase compared to larger chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by replication timing analysis in Figure 2D-E, which shows statistically significant differences (p<0.0001) between chromosome size groups. The correlation between chromosome size and replication timing is clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical testing.

results.result: AcH3, base J, and KKT1 co-localize at a single locus per chromosome corresponding to ES MFA-seq peaks, including at six transcription termination sites where AcH3 enrichment was not predicted.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C64-C66 are well-supported by ChIP data analysis in Figure 3A-C showing co-localization at ES MFA-seq peaks. The unexpected finding of AcH3 at termination sites is documented, though the modest enrichment suggests this may be functionally distinct from canonical AcH3 sites.

results.result: The simultaneous presence of AcH3, base J, and KKT1 drives coordinated DNA replication initiation specifically in early S phase, while base J alone shows little correlation with DNA replication in any cell cycle stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by meta-analysis in Figure 3C showing strong MFA-seq signal at AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites only in ES phase, and minimal signal at base J-only sites. The temporal specificity and lack of base J correlation are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Subtelomeric AcH3 sites show stronger and broader MFA-seq signals than chromosome-internal AcH3 sites, with relatively higher usage during G1, indicating that local chromatin environment modulates DNA replication initiation timing.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C77 are supported by meta-analysis in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing differential MFA-seq signal amplitude and timing between internal and end AcH3 sites. The conclusion about chromatin environment is a reasonable inference from the spatial and temporal differences observed.

results.result: No specific DNA sequence signature correlates with regions of DNA replication initiation in L. major.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by the negative result from MEME analysis. While negative results require careful interpretation, this is consistent with findings in other eukaryotes (C145) and the authors appropriately report the absence of sequence-specific motifs.

results.result: Highly localized G/T skew polarity changes demarcate DNA replication initiation sites at AcH3/base J/KKT1 loci and subtelomeric AcH3 sites, distinct from the broader transcription-associated skew patterns, providing evidence for replication initiation at central regions of all 36 chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C88 are well-supported by skew analysis in Figure 4A-C showing localized polarity changes at replication sites distinct from transcription-associated patterns. The differential patterns between internal and subtelomeric sites support the inference of extensive initiation at subtelomeres but not internal AcH3 sites.

results.result: G4 quadruplexes show strand-specific distribution patterns around DNA replication initiation sites, with distinct arrangements at AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites (asymmetric upstream/downstream) versus AcH3/base J and base J sites (symmetric), reflecting spatial and temporal differences in replication activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C97 are supported by G4 distribution analysis in Figure 4B,D showing striking correlation with skew polarity changes and distinct patterns at different chromatin contexts. The strand-specific arrangement and correlation with replication sites are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: At chromosome-central AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites, G/T skew and G4 patterns are dictated by the leading strand of bidirectional replication forks, with leading strand replication and transcription always co-directional, suggesting selective pressure to avoid replisome-polymerase collisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 are supported by analysis in Figure 5B-D showing consistent patterns regardless of transcription configuration. The co-directionality is clearly demonstrated, though the inference about selective pressure, while reasonable, is speculative and would benefit from additional evolutionary or functional evidence.

results.result: L. major has very limited capacity to activate dormant origins in ES phase under replication stress, with only three new sites detected after HU treatment, all at transcription boundaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by HU treatment data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The limited activation of backup origins is clearly demonstrated, though the biological significance of this finding depends on whether the HU concentration used is physiologically relevant.

results.result: Subtelomeric DNA replication is sensitive to hydroxyurea treatment while chromosome-internal replication at AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites is largely unaffected, with HU-induced loss of replication signal extending ~50 kb from chromosome ends.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C105-C112 are well-supported by HU treatment experiments in Figure 6B-D showing differential sensitivity between subtelomeric and internal sites. The spatial extent of the effect is quantified. This provides strong evidence for mechanistic differences between the two replication modes.

results.result: Subtelomeric DNA replication requires the 9-1-1 complex (RAD9 and HUS1), while chromosome-internal replication at AcH3/base J/KKT1 sites does not, with RAD9+/- showing dramatic loss of subtelomeric signal and HUS1+/- showing milder effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C114-C120 are strongly supported by mutant analysis in Figure 7A-C showing selective loss of subtelomeric but not internal replication in RAD9+/- and HUS1+/- cells. The differential requirement provides compelling evidence for mechanistically distinct replication processes. The milder HUS1 phenotype suggests potential functional redundancy or dosage effects.

results.result: L. major genome duplication employs a bimodal program with predominantly chromosome-internal initiation in early S phase supplemented by subtelomeric replication that possibly extends beyond S phase, with chromosomes rarely completing replication by the end of S phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C121-C123 represent the main conclusions integrating all MFA-seq data. The bimodal program is well-supported by the combined evidence. However, the claim that replication extends beyond S phase (C12, C122) is inferred from detection in G2/M and G1 enriched populations, which may still contain some S phase cells despite enrichment. Additional cell cycle markers would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Previous MFA-seq work detected only a single DNA replication initiation region per chromosome in Leishmania, predicted to be insufficient for complete genome duplication and unprecedented in eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C21-C22, C24 accurately represent prior work (Marques et al., 2015) and its implications. The current study resolves this apparent insufficiency by discovering subtelomeric replication. This contextualizes the significance of the current findings.

results.result: SNS-seq detected thousands of DNA synthesis initiation sites in Leishmania, revealing a huge dichotomy with MFA-seq mapping that detected only single sites per chromosome.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 accurately represent the discrepancy between prior MFA-seq and SNS-seq studies. The current work partially resolves this by detecting subtelomeric sites, though a quantitative gap remains. The authors appropriately acknowledge this in C153.

results.result: L. major exhibits constitutive mosaic aneuploidy and achieves genome duplication using DNA replication extending beyond S phase, suggesting that mitosis before complete genome duplication may not be inherently problematic in eukaryotes and may explain widespread aneuploidy.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129, C131 involve speculation about the relationship between post-S phase replication and aneuploidy. While C127 is supported by citations, C128-C129 are speculative interpretations. The causal relationship between replication timing and aneuploidy is not directly tested and represents a hypothesis for future work.

results.result: If a cell cycle checkpoint exists in Leishmania, it must be permissive enough to allow mitosis with ongoing DNA replication, possibly involving the 9-1-1 complex in a subtelomere-specific checkpoint.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 are speculative inferences about checkpoint mechanisms. While the observation of replication in G2/M is supported, the mechanistic interpretation about checkpoint permissiveness and 9-1-1 function is hypothetical and requires direct testing of checkpoint activity.

results.result: The relationship between MFA-seq peaks and ORC binding sites remains undetermined in L. major, with subtelomeric replication potentially deriving from DNA repair rather than ORC-dependent origins, as suggested by RAD9 dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C144 acknowledge important gaps in understanding the molecular mechanisms. C139-C141 provide circumstantial evidence for ORC involvement at internal sites, but C142-C144 regarding subtelomeric mechanisms are speculative. Direct ORC mapping and functional studies are needed.

results.result: DNA replication initiation in L. major is not associated with specific DNA sequences but is coupled with transcription activity at boundaries of multigene transcription units, similar to patterns in other eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C147 are supported by the absence of sequence motifs (C79) and consistent localization to transcription boundaries (C40). The comparison to other eukaryotes is appropriately cited, though the authors note mechanisms may differ.

results.result: The temporal order of AcH3, base J, and KKT1 deposition during the cell cycle may be a major determinant of DNA replication initiation outcomes, though current ChIP datasets lack cell cycle resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C149 identify an important limitation and propose a testable hypothesis. C148 is factual about data limitations, while C149 is speculative. This represents an important direction for future work but is not tested in the current study.

results.result: The modified MFA-seq approach using exponentially growing versus stationary cells is convenient and cost-effective, partially explains DNA combing observations, and reveals that subtelomeric replication is a core component of genome transmission in Leishmania.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C154 are supported by the successful application of the method and the novel findings it enabled. C152 is a valid methodological contribution, C153 appropriately acknowledges partial resolution of prior discrepancies, and C154 represents the main conclusion about biological significance.
